title_en: Buying a Train Ticket in Chinese

sentences.en: Tomorrow my friend and I are taking the train to Beijing, so we go to the station to buy tickets.
The clerk asks, "Where are you going?"
I say, "To Beijing — two tickets for the nine o'clock, please."
The clerk checks and says, "The nine o'clock is sold out. Would ten work?"
I check with my friend, who says, "That's fine — ten isn't late either."
The clerk says, "Alright — two tickets, forty kuai in total."
We buy the tickets, and on the way out my friend says, "Let's get here a bit early tomorrow."

quiz.q: Where are the two friends going?
Why can't they take the nine o'clock train?
a: It does not go to Beijing

quiz.q: How much do the two tickets cost in total?

grammar.p: 几点的 — "the one at what time"
grammar.e: 的 turns a time into "the one at that time", so you can drop the noun: 九点的 = the nine o'clock one.
grammar.x: 我们要九点的票。 — We want tickets for the nine o'clock.

grammar.p: 张 — measure word for flat things
grammar.e: Tickets, paper and tables take 张, never 个: 两张票, not 两个票.
grammar.x: 两张票，一共六十块。 — Two tickets, sixty kuai in total.

grammar.e: 别 makes a soft negative command, gentler than 不要. It appears all over spoken Chinese.
grammar.x: 别说了。 — Stop talking / don't say any more.
